method: MIXED, and the two halves cover DIFFERENT CONDITIONS. A1-A3 are AMH pages on ORTHOSTATIC HYPOTENSION, paraphrased, no passage stored. S1 is the OPEN RACGP AJGP case study 'A dizzying diagnosis' (December 2025) on POSTURAL ORTHOSTATIC TACHYCARDIA SYNDROME, quoted verbatim including its dose table. POTS is defined partly by the ABSENCE of orthostatic hypotension, so the two are placed side by side deliberately and their doses are NOT interchangeable -- AMH gives midodrine THREE times daily for orthostatic hypotension and S1 gives it TWICE daily for POTS. That difference is stated, not averaged.

claims.claim: POTS is a multi-system disorder of orthostatic intolerance, particularly a rise in heart rate on standing, WITHOUT marked orthostatic hypotension or another cause for tachycardia; palpitations, weakness or lightheadedness improve on sitting
claims.source_text: POTS is a multi-system disorder characterised by symptoms of orthostatic intolerance, particularly a rise in HR when standing, without marked orthostatic hypotension or concomitant cause for tachycardia. … Patients often experience palpitations, weakness or lightheadedness, which improve upon being seated.
claims.locator: RACGP, Australian Journal of General Practice, 'A dizzying diagnosis', Sadhvi SS, Naresh B, Wu TT, Kwan A, Volume 54 Issue 12, December 2025, doi 10.31128/AJGP-03-25-7592, at https://www1.racgp.org.au/ajgp/2025/december/a-dizzying-diagnosis, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Up to 80% of POTS patients are female, often from a White background, and the most common age of symptom onset is 14 years with a mean age of 21 plus or minus 12 years

claims.claim: All FOUR of the 2015 Heart Rhythm Society criteria must be met to diagnose POTS: a sustained heart rate increase of at least 30 bpm, or at least 40 bpm if aged 12 to 19 years, within 10 minutes of upright posture; ABSENCE of an orthostatic BP drop of 20/10 mmHg or more; symptoms of orthostatic intolerance worse upright with rapid improvement on lying down, for more than 6 months; and absence of other conditions that could explain sinus tachycardia
claims.source_text: sustained HR increase of ≥30 bpm (or ≥40 bpm if the patient is aged 12-19 years) within 10 minutes of upright posture … absence of orthostatic BP drop ≥20/10 mmHg … symptoms of orthostatic intolerance that are worse while upright, with rapid improvement upon return to a supine position for > 6 months … absence of other conditions that could explain sinus tachycardia
claims.locator: RACGP, Australian Journal of General Practice, 'A dizzying diagnosis', Sadhvi SS, Naresh B, Wu TT, Kwan A, Volume 54 Issue 12, December 2025, doi 10.31128/AJGP-03-25-7592, at https://www1.racgp.org.au/ajgp/2025/december/a-dizzying-diagnosis, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Three main pathophysiologies underlie POTS: autonomic neuropathy, hypovolaemia and a hyperadrenergic state; autonomic neuropathy of small postganglionic sudomotor fibres, mainly in the feet, is reported in up to 50% of POTS patients
claims.source_text: Three main pathophysiologies that underlie POTS are: (1) autonomic neuropathy; (2) hypovolemia; and (3) a hyperadrenergic state. … Autonomic neuropathy of small postganglionic sudomotor fibres, mainly in the feet, have been reported in up to 50% of POTS patients.
claims.locator: RACGP, Australian Journal of General Practice, 'A dizzying diagnosis', Sadhvi SS, Naresh B, Wu TT, Kwan A, Volume 54 Issue 12, December 2025, doi 10.31128/AJGP-03-25-7592, at https://www1.racgp.org.au/ajgp/2025/december/a-dizzying-diagnosis, retrieved 2026-09-22

claims.claim: Hypovolaemic POTS is characterised by low plasma blood volume and a 24-hour urine sodium below 100 mmol/L; hyperadrenergic POTS by a rise in systolic BP above 10 mmHg during a 10-minute tilt table test and a plasma noradrenaline above 600 pg/mL
